newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Prospect of new monarchy doesn't thrill Albanians.
newsitem.headline: Prospect of new monarchy doesn't thrill Albanians.

text.p: King Leka I, back from life-long exile to seek a restoration of the monarchy in chaotic Albania with promises of calm and order, has found scant support among impoverished voters.

Whether Leka Zogu, 58, can turn his dream into reality will be decided in a referendum to be held alongside Sunday's parliamentary elections, widely seen as the only hope to restore peace after months of violence.
The bespectacled king, towering over most of his countrymen at 2.04 metres (six feet eight inches), has toured Albania for several weeks.
Leka wins praise for being above the dirty politics many voters associate with their leaders.

But he has failed to drum up much support even though many Albanians blame President Sali Berisha for months of calamity triggered by the collapse of five shady pyramid investment schemes that left them penniless.
Others blame the opposition Socialists for this Balkan country's instability.
"What we are asking for is not monarchy...what we want is democracy and some leaders who respect it," said Mira Llaziku, 31, a teacher in the southern town of Gjirokaster.

"I will vote for him (Leka) because he is clean, unlike other politicians in Albania these days," said Merita, 19, in the southern port town of Vlore, focal point of the unrest that swept the country. "But can he really do anything for us?"

Leka was just two days old when his father King Zog I fled Albania before the mountainous country was invaded by Italian fascists in 1942. He was barred from returning to his homeland by the post-war Communist regime.
Zog died in Paris in 1961. Leka says he was automatically proclaimed king based on the 1928 constitution.

Leka is trying hard to evoke images of his late father, remembered by many Albanians as a powerful figure who quelled deep-rooted tribal, regional and secular rivalries while improving education and infrastructure.

"We need this man at the top so that our dirty politicians don't fight each other for the president's chair," an elderly man said during a campaign rally Leka held at Tirana's main Skanderbeg Square, attended by 3,000 flag-waving supporters.
The king, who sees himself as a unifying factor in a country shattered by months of lawlessness, told the crowd he would deliver "peace, unity and brotherhood".
He is backed by the pro-monarchy Movement of Legality, which won some five percent in local elections last October.

Party leader Guri Durollari says the king could help restore peace and stability but admits it is difficult to judge support for him in a country he left as an infant. Some Albanians believe he may do better in the countryside than in cities like Tirana.

Leka now lives with his mother Geraldina, wife Suzana and son Leka in South Africa. When he attempted to visit his homeland for the first time in 1993, he was bundled back on to a private aircraft within 24 hours of his arrival on grounds that his passport, marked "Kingdom of Albania", was invalid.

"We tried Zog, Enver Hoxha's difficult Communist regime and Berisha who took all our money and hopes," said a middle-aged Albanian who works at a Western embassy. "Now we need a strong government and a president like the ones in Germany or Italy."
Albania emerged in 1990 from 45 years of Stalinist isolation under dictator Hoxha.

The country made some headway towards building a market economy before the unrest. But many Albanians say Leka's television campaign promises to turn Tirana into a capital akin to London, Stockholm or Madrid are little more than hot air.
"How can you compare life in today's Tirana with London or Madrid?" said Arban, a 25-year old unemployed graduate. "For the moment, that is beyond our wildest imagination."
